scenario.name: Unit 42 — Operation MidnightEclipse: PAN-OS GlobalProtect RCE & UPSTYLE Backdoor
scenario.shortSubtitle: Palo Alto Unit 42 · CVE-2024-3400 Telemetry Cron Injection & system.pth Persistence
scenario.overview: Imagine a brick city apartment building entrance with a glass vestibule, a wall of brass resident mailboxes, a doorman podium, and a glowing brass intercom buzzer panel. Standing outside the locked glass apartment vestibule, an uninvited caller presses a crafted sequence on the brass intercom buzzer pretending to be building maintenance. In this real-world scenario, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the building doorman's station, then leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the apartment lobby later. The doorman checks the visitor sign-in ledger against the intercom buzz history and realizes no maintenance visit was ever scheduled by management. In this scenario (CVE-2024-3400, Unit 42, Operation MidnightEclipse: PAN-OS GlobalProtect RCE & UPSTYLE Backdoor), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: directory Traversal in the "SESSID" Cookie, then the Root Telemetry Cron Job Executes, then deploying the "UPSTYLE" Python Webshell. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Directory Traversal in the "SESSID" Cookie, then The Root Telemetry Cron Job Executes, then Deploying the "UPSTYLE" Python Webshell, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

details.description: UTA0218 operator sending crafted HTTP POST requests to GlobalProtect with shell backticks embedded in the SESSID cookie header.
Internet-facing GlobalProtect portal where malformed SESSID cookies create arbitrary filenames in the device_telemetry minute directory.
UPSTYLE persistence script loaded automatically by Python via system.pth, parsing img[...] regex commands from sslvpn-access.log.
PAN-OS configuration repository extracted by the attacker and written to bootstrap.min.css for unauthenticated HTTP retrieval before restoration.
Monitors PAN-OS gpsvc logs, unexpected zero-byte files in device_telemetry/minute, and Python .pth startup modifications.

memoryBlocks.description: In-memory Python thread spawned by system.pth watching sslvpn-access.log for img[...] base64 commands.

stages.title: SESSID COOKIE PATH TRAVERSAL (CVE-2024-3400)
stages.subtitle: Arbitrary file creation in /opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/
stages.description: Standing outside the locked glass apartment vestibule, an uninvited caller presses a crafted sequence on the brass intercom buzzer pretending to be building maintenance. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the building doorman's station while everyday visitors and the building doorman go about their routine. The attacker sends an unauthenticated HTTPS POST request to /ssl-vpn/hipreport.esp (the Host Information Profile endpoint on the GlobalProtect VPN portal, which is reachable from the internet before a user finishes logging in). Instead of a normal session ID, the Cookie: SESSID= header contains ../../../../opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/aacurl ... | sh (where the "../" path traversal climbs out of the session folder into the firewall’s telemetry queue directory, and the backticks ... embed a Linux shell command directly inside the filename itself). When GlobalProtect processes hipreport.esp, its session serializer calls fopen() using the raw SESSID cookie value as the file path without stripping "../" sequences (creating an empty 0-byte file on disk, which is all the attacker needs, because the exploit payload lives inside the file’s name, not its contents). Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SESSID TRAVERSAL / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 UTA0218 Threat Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM).

stages.title: TELEMETRY CRON SHELL EXECUTION (DT_CURL)
stages.subtitle: Root cron job passes unsanitized filename to shell
stages.description: Fooled by the caller’s voice over the lobby intercom, the building doorman buzzes open the interior lobby door and reads out the hallway elevator code. Here in Step 2 inside the apartment lobby, the intruder uses borrowed access inside the apartment lobby to slip closer to the brass intercom buzzer & elevator without disturbing the resident locked mailboxes. Once every minute, the PAN-OS device telemetry cron job (dt_curl / sendTelemetry, a scheduled background script running with full uid=0(root) privileges) loops through every file in /opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/ and pastes each filename directly into a shell command string without escaping special characters. When the Linux shell parses that command string, it sees the backticks (curl ... | sh, which in Bash/sh means "execute the command inside these backticks first and substitute its output"), immediately running the attacker’s payload as root. Because the attacker never needed to write data into the file, only control its filename via the Step 1 path traversal, even a 0-byte file in the minute/ telemetry folder triggers unauthenticated root Remote Code Execution the next time the cron job ticks. In the documented Auditd SYSCALL 59 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge, PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the CRON RCE (ROOT) request succeeded on PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 UPSTYLE PYTHON .PTH PERSISTENCE & LOG C2). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CRON RCE (ROOT) / ⇠#2 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM).

stages.title: UPSTYLE PYTHON .PTH PERSISTENCE & LOG C2
stages.subtitle: Writing system.pth and parsing sslvpn-access.log for img[...] commands
stages.description: Slipping past the brass resident mailboxes straight into the elevator, the intruder gains access to private upper-floor corridors without ever owning an apartment key. In this final step inside the apartment lobby, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the apartment lobby later until the doorman visitor sign-in book catches the mismatch. Combining Volexity’s and Unit 42’s forensic findings: with root access on the firewall, the attacker steals /opt/pancfg/mgmt/saved-configs/running-config.xml (the master PAN-OS configuration file containing VPN pre-shared keys, administrator hashes, and internal network routes used by UTA0218 to pivot into internal Windows Domain Controllers via SMB/winexe) and injects the UPSTYLE Python backdoor into /usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/system.pth (a Python path-configuration file that Python automatically executes every time any system script starts on the appliance). UPSTYLE monitors /var/log/pan/sslvpn_ngx_error.log for crafted HTTPS requests and writes command output into /var/appweb/sslvpndocs/global-protect/portal/css/bootstrap.min.css (the public CSS stylesheet of the VPN login page, letting the attacker read command results over port 443). When the attacker sends a specially formatted HTTPS request with a bogus URL that logs an error into sslvpn_ngx_error.log, the background UPSTYLE inotify daemon parses the embedded Base64 command, appends the output inside a CSS comment /*...*/ in bootstrap.min.css, and 15 seconds later restores the original CSS file and deletes the offending log line (erasing both the command and output traces). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SYSTEM.PTH HOOK / ⇠#3 ACK 4,128 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge) to Node ④ (#4 UPSTYLE Python Backdoor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM).

detectionRule.title: PAN-OS Telemetry Cron Spawning Outbound Curl / Python Stager
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: PAN-OS CVE-2024-3400 Root Telemetry Command Injection
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: auditd
detection:
  selection:
    type: 'EXECVE'
    a2|contains:
      - 'device_telemetry'
      - 'update.py'
      - 'system.pth'
  condition: selection
level: critical

detectionRule.title: Unit 42 Official YARA — Python UPSTYLE Backdoor (system.pth)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
rule PaloAlto_Unit42_UPSTYLE_Backdoor {
  meta:
    author = "Palo Alto Networks Unit 42"
    reference = "Operation MidnightEclipse CVE-2024-3400"
  strings:
    $s1 = "/var/log/pan/sslvpn-access.log" ascii
    $s2 = "/var/appweb/sslvpndocs/global-protect/portal/css/bootstrap.min.css" ascii
    $s3 = "img\\[([a-zA-Z0-9+/=]+)\\]" ascii
    $s4 = "/proc/self/cmdline" ascii
  condition:
    3 of ($s*)
}
detectionRule.mitigation: Perform a factory reset and redeploy compromised PAN-OS images; rotate all device credentials and private certificates stored in running-config.xml.
